description: Since 1951, one rule has protected persecuted people all over the world. But it never anticipated today's migration crises.

hero.hook: Since 1951, one rule has protected the persecuted everywhere. But it never saw the climate coming.

blocks.text: All over the world, people flee their country because their life or their freedom is under threat. For centuries an unwritten rule has said that a door must be opened to them: the **right of asylum**. Governed by precise laws since the 20th century, that door is now more and more contested.

The modern legal framework of asylum rests on the **[[Geneva Convention]]** of 1951, written after the Second World War, when millions of people were still wandering across Europe. Limited to Europe at first, it became universal in 1967 thanks to an additional protocol.

The Convention gives a precise definition of the word **refugee**: a person outside their own country who cannot return for fear of persecution because of race, religion, nationality, membership of a social group, or political opinion. That definition troublingly leaves out the victims of natural disasters and famine.

At the core of this protection is the **[[principle of non-refoulement]]**: it forbids sending anyone back to a place where they would risk torture or death. To see that it is applied, the United Nations relies on **[[UNHCR]]**, an agency that specializes in protecting uprooted people.

We often picture the reception of refugees as a burden carried by rich countries. In fact, about 75% of the world's refugees are hosted by low- and middle-income countries close to the conflict zones.

In public debate the words migrant and refugee are often mixed up, yet they describe different legal situations. An **asylum seeker** has filed a request for protection and is waiting for an authority to examine it. If the answer is positive, that person officially becomes a **refugee**, with the right to stay for the long term and to work.

An **economic migrant**, by contrast, leaves home voluntarily to look for a better life, and the Geneva Convention does not apply. The distinction fuels political tension, because real journeys often mix both motives, and reviewing a claim can take years, during which applicants are usually barred from working.

sections.title: Refugee, asylum seeker, migrant: three different words

blocks.text: **2015** was a turning point for Europe: more than a million people crossed the Mediterranean, most of them fleeing the civil war in Syria. That influx exposed the flaws of the **[[Dublin Regulation]]**, which makes the first country of arrival handle every claim, overloading Greece and Italy.

blocks.caption: In 2015, more than a million people crossed the Mediterranean to reach Europe

blocks.text: Europe answered the crisis in scattered fashion. In 2016, a deal between the EU and Turkey offered a trade-off: in exchange for financial aid, Turkey agreed to block departures for Europe, a strategy criticized for possibly ignoring non-refoulement. In 2024, the EU adopted a new pact on migration, looking for a balance between solidarity and border control.
One of the most famous refugees in history is Albert Einstein. In 1933, threatened by the Nazis because he was Jewish, he gave up his German citizenship and was granted asylum in the United States.

sections.title: 2015: the shock of the European migration crisis

blocks.text: The future of asylum runs into something the drafters of 1951 never imagined: the climate crisis. By 2050, hundreds of millions of people could be displaced by rising seas or by the spread of deserts. Yet no status of climate refugee exists, because these people cannot prove “persecution” in the sense of the Convention.

Asylum is also becoming a more and more political subject in Western democracies: procedures are hardening, and the idea of protection that is only temporary is gaining ground over the idea of lasting integration.

The 1951 Geneva Convention protects people persecuted for political, religious or social reasons, through the principle of non-refoulement. But it remains poorly suited to the new flows of climate refugees and to today's migration crises, where causes are mixed.

sections.title: The new challenge: climate and politics
